newsitem.title: USA: Ford's U.S. February sales drop, Toyota sales rise.
newsitem.headline: Ford's U.S. February sales drop, Toyota sales rise.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. capped a down month for the Big Three U.S. automakers by reporting a 3.2 percent drop in February sales on Tuesday, while Toyota Motor Corp.'s sales rose 17 percent to a record high for the month.
"I think the message of February's results is the Japanese resurgence is here to stay," said John Casesa, an analyst at Schroder Wertheim.

Ford's sales of light trucks, including minivans, sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks, rose 1.5 percent from February 1996 to 163,117. But car sales at the nation's No. 2 automaker continued to slump, falling 8.5 percent to 128,945.

Overall light vehicle sales at Ford slid to 292,062 from 314,223 in February 1996. The percentage changes are based on the average daily selling rate, instead of the monthly totals. February had 24 selling days, one less than a year ago.

Ford's sport utility vehicle sales were held back by short supplies of the Expedition due to a three-week strike by a seat-maker that disrupted prodution. Inventories will remain tight in March because of the time it takes to retrofit Expeditions with seats, Ford said.
On Monday, General Motors Corp. posted light vehicle sales of 352,234, a decline of 7.4 percent for the month, while Chrysler Corp. sales were down 2.8 percent to 193,983.

In a sign of how foreign automakers dominated February sales, imported car sales rose nearly 15 percent and imported light trucks shot up about 31 percent. Domestically produced cars sales fell 5 percent; domestically made trucks slipped 1.1 percent.

The industry as a whole finished the month with 1,153,972 units, a decline of 0.9 percent against a difficult comparison a year ago. The seasonally adjusted annual selling rate for February was 15.3 million units, down from 15.7 million last year, the strongest month in all of 1996.

Propelled by its Camry sedan, Toyota division car sales jumped 20.9 percent to 54,632. Camry sales rose 27 percent to 28,127, marking the second month in a row that it was the best-selling car in the United States.
Meanwhile, Toyota's 4Runner and RAV4 sport utility vehicles had sales increases of 12.3 percent and 16.4 percent, respectively, both records for February. Total Toyota sales were 86,007 vs. 76,485.

Japanese automakers again posted market share gains in February from a year ago, capturing about 23 percent of the market vs. 20.7 percent last year. The Big Three's share fell about three points to 72.7 percent.

Bob Rewey, Ford's group vice president of marketing and sales, blamed weak car sales on the growing popularity of trucks. He also said the Japanese were using the yen's weakness to boost their incentives and seize car market share.

That was disputed by Yale Gieszl, executive vice president of Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A. Inc. He attributed Toyota's success to its strong product lineup, and claimed the company had reduced incentives in February from last year.
"Our competitors have been slow to launch new products," he said in a statement.

But Casesa at Schroder Wertheim said the Japanese automakers were in fact taking advantage of the weak yen to price aggressively. At the same time, they were reaping the rewards of high product quality, which provides strong residual values and allows them to lower lease prices.
Other companies reporting Tuesday include: Mazda Motor Corp., whose U.S. sales fell 16.4 percent to 15,333; Isuzu

Motor Co. Ltd. sales were down 17 percent to 6,531; Volkswagen of America Inc. sales were up 6.5 percent to 9,249; and VW's Audi of America Inc. unit had sales of 2,448, a 31 percent jump that represents its best February sales in 11 years.
